Sitges Carnival & Pride: Where to Recharge Before and After the Parties

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 8:50
Instaread

Twice a year, Sitges turns up the volume. In late winter, Carnival takes over the streets with sequins, feathers and parades that run until dawn. In early summer, Sitges Pride fills the seafront with music, flags and one of the most joyful crowds on the Mediterranean. Both are bucket-list events for gay travellers and both can leave you in serious need of a proper rest. This guide covers what to expect from Sitges’ two biggest celebrations, how to plan your trip around them, and why adding a few quiet days before or after the festivities may be the smartest move you make.

Sitges Carnival: a week without limits

Sitges Carnival is one of the most famous in Spain, and the gay community is at the heart of it. Celebrations usually take place in February or early March, in the week before Lent, so check the dates for your year before
booking.

What to expect

Elaborate parades: the two big night parades, the Rua de la Disbauxa (“Debauchery Parade”) and the Rua de l’Extermini (“Extermination Parade”) are the highlights, with dozens of floats and thousands of dancers in costume.
Costumes everywhere: from simple masks to full drag couture, dressing up is expected, not optional.
Late nights: bars and clubs stay busy until the early hours, and the streets stay lively well after the parades end.

Tips for Carnival

Book accommodation well in advance; the town fills up quickly.
Plan your costume before you travel; local shops sell out.
Pace yourself: the main parades fall on different nights, so you do not need to go out every night to see the best of it.

Sitges Pride: sun, sea and celebration

Sitges Pride usually takes place in June and combines the energy of a big Pride with the setting of a beach town. Expect a colourful parade along the seafront, outdoor concerts, beach parties and a packed calendar of events in the bars of Carrer Joan Tarrida and Carrer del Primer de Maig.

Tips for Pride

The sun is strong in June: bring sunscreen, a hat and plenty of water.
The seafront parade draws big crowds, so arrive early for a good spot.
Daytime is for the beach, Bassa Rodona is the town’s best-known gay beach.

What to pack for festival week

Packing for Sitges during Carnival or Pride is a little different from packing for a regular beach break. A few
essentials will make your trip much easier.

Costumes and accessories: for Carnival, bring more than one look, the parades and parties run over several nights. Glitter, wigs and comfortable shoes are a must.
Beachwear and sun protection: for Pride, a good hat, sunglasses and high-factor sunscreen are as important as your outfit.
Comfortable footwear: Sitges’ old town is hilly and partly cobbled, and you will be on your feet for hours.
Earplugs and an eye mask: if you stay in the centre, the streets can be loud until well after sunrise.
Walking shoes and a light jacket: for the quiet days in the hills, and because February nights by the sea can be cool, even in Catalonia.

Eat like a local

Good food is the best cure for a long night. Sitges and the surrounding Garraf region have their own culinary
traditions worth discovering.

Xató: a winter salad of endive, salt cod, tuna and anchovies dressed with a rich romesco-style sauce. It is a local speciality, especially popular around Carnival season.
Malvasia de Sitges: a sweet, historic dessert wine produced in the town for centuries, perfect with a slow lunch.
Cava from the Penedès: the region’s sparkling wine is made just inland from Sitges, so it is always on the menu.
Seafood and rice dishes: from paella to fideuà, the seafront restaurants are ideal for a long, late lunch.

Book lunch reservations during festival weeks, and remember that Spanish meal times are late: lunch often starts around 2pm and dinner rarely before 9pm.

Other dates for your calendar

Carnival and Pride are the headliners, but Sitges hosts other popular events for the community, including Bear
Week in September. The Sitges Film Festival in October also brings a buzz to town. Outside these dates, Sitges is
calmer, with more locals and a slower pace, perfect if you want the beach without the crowds. For bars, beaches and the best of gay Sitges all year round, see this complete gay guide to Sitges.

Why your trip needs quiet days, too

Festival weeks are intense. Late nights, loud music and packed streets are part of the fun, but after a few days
most of us need sleep, silence and somewhere to lie in the sun without a sound system next door. That is why more and more travellers plan their festival trip in two parts: a few nights in the heart of Sitges for the parades and the parties, and a few days somewhere that feels like the complete opposite, either before the celebrations begin or once they are over.

There is a practical side to this, too. During Carnival and Pride, hotels in the centre of Sitges often require
minimum stays and charge peak prices, and rooms close to the main streets can be noisy at all hours. Keeping
your in-town stay to the core party nights, and spending the rest of your holiday somewhere calmer, gives you
more space, better sleep and a much more relaxed trip.

Before the parties: arrive and adjust

Flying in from London, New York or further afield and heading straight into festival week is a recipe for watching
the best parade half asleep. Two or three quiet days first let you shake off the jet lag, find your rhythm and
arrive in town rested, with energy to spare for the nights that matter.

After the parties: the soft landing

When the last parade is over, resist the urge to fly home exhausted. A few slow days afterward, real sleep,
mountain air, long lunches and nothing on the schedule, turn a great festival into a genuinely great holiday,
and send you home recharged rather than wrecked.

The countryside option: the hills of the Garraf

Behind Sitges, the landscape changes quickly. Within minutes you are among limestone hills, pine trees and
small villages in the Garraf, with the Penedès wine region just beyond. It is quiet, green and a world away from
the festival crowds.

This is where Casa Brisa, a boutique guesthouse exclusively for gay men, is located in the village of Olivella, a
short drive from the Sitges seafront. It is a small property with four accommodation options and an outdoor
pool, designed for guests who want calm surroundings, privacy and time to rest. Clothing is optional around the
pool and sunbathing areas; indoor shared spaces remain clothed.

Casa Brisa is not designed as a base for nights out in town, and that is exactly the point. It is the place to come
before the celebrations, to arrive in Sitges rested, or after them, to slow down, sleep properly and enjoy the
quieter side of the Catalan coast.

A recharge day in the Garraf

Morning: a slow breakfast and no alarm clock.
Midday: a walk in the Garraf hills, or a long lunch in a village restaurant.
Afternoon: time by the pool in summer, or a visit to a Penedès cava cellar in winter.
Evening: a glass of local wine at sunset, a quiet dinner and an early night.

Getting around

Sitges is easy to reach from Barcelona by train in around 40 minutes, and the town centre is walkable. The countryside around it is a different story: villages in the Garraf are residential and spread out, so a car makes life
much easier, and it opens up the vineyards, hiking trails and coastal villages of the region. If you are splitting your stay, plan the move between town and countryside for the daytime: check out of your Sitges hotel in the morning, drive up through the hills in daylight, and leave the parade nights to the people staying within walking distance of the action.

Final thoughts

Sitges Carnival and Pride are two of the best reasons to visit this corner of Catalonia, and they deserve to be enjoyed at full energy. The trick is to give yourself time on either side of them. Arrive rested, dance until sunrise in town, then retreat to the hills to sleep in and slow down. That is how you get the most out of Sitges’ biggest
weeks.

And if you fall in love with the area, as many visitors do, come back outside festival season too. With the
crowds gone, Sitges and the Garraf countryside show a gentler side: quiet beaches, long lunches, vineyard visits
and evenings that end with a glass of cava rather than a sunrise.
